evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the study

claim: PGE2 is likely to predominantly exert its effects via the EP2/4 receptors in normal β-cells
source: PGE2 is likely to predominantly exert its effects via the EP2/4 receptors in normal β-cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that EP2/4 receptors mediate PGE2 effects in normal β-cells

claim: In instances of established β-cell dysfunction, such as in T2DM, it appears that PGE2 may act through the upregulated EP3 receptors
source: However, in instances of established β-cell dysfunction, such as in T2DM, it appears that PGE2 may act through the upregulated EP3 receptors (Kimple et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kimple et al., 2013 and is inferred from the discussion of EP3 upregulation in T2DM

claim: Both Kv2.1 and Kv2.2 contribute to the delayed outward K+ current in human β-cells
source: Both Kv2.1 and Kv2.2 contribute to the delayed outward K+ current in human β-cells, and their mRNA expression in diabetic islets is lower than that in nondiabetic islets (Fu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fu et al., 2017

claim: The mRNA expression of Kv2.1 and Kv2.2 in diabetic islets is lower than that in nondiabetic islets
source: Both Kv2.1 and Kv2.2 contribute to the delayed outward K+ current in human β-cells, and their mRNA expression in diabetic islets is lower than that in nondiabetic islets (Fu et al., 2017).

claim: Kv2.1 channels in cell membrane exist in two forms: clustered and non-clustered

claim: Non-clustered Kv2.1 channels conduct K+ normally, while clustered Kv2.1 channels are barely conductive

claim: Kv2.1 channels form clusters in INS-1(832/13) cells and human β-cells

claim: Kv2.1-mediated insulin exocytosis requires Kv2.1 clustering and a direct interaction with syntaxin 1A but is not dependent on its electrical function
source: Kv2.1-mediated insulin exocytosis requires Kv2.1 clustering and a direct interaction with syntaxin 1A but is not dependent on its electrical function (Dai et al., 2012; Fu et al., 2017).

claim: Kv2.2 channels play a crucial role in maintaining repetitive AP firing by promoting the recovery of voltage-gated sodium channels from inactivation

claim: Inhibition of Kv2.2 channels significantly reduces the repetitive firing in medial nucleus of the trapezoid body neurons and cortical pyramidal neurons
source: Inhibition of Kv2.2 channels significantly reduces the repetitive firing in medial nucleus of the trapezoid body neurons and cortical pyramidal neurons (Johnston et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2024).

claim: The major effect of PGE2-induced inhibition of Kv2.2 is to reduce the firing rate in β-cells
source: In the present study, we found that the major effect of PGE2-induced inhibition of Kv2.2 is to reduce the firing rate in β-cells, suggesting that Kv2.2 plays a key role in the β-cell repetitive firing upon stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the study

claim: Kv2.2 plays a key role in the β-cell repetitive firing upon stimulation

claim: The PGE2-induced reduction in β-cell repetitive firing would decrease calcium channel opening, and, thus, insulin secretion

claim: The activation of Gi/o protein-coupled receptors leads to the stimulation of Na+/K+ ATPase
source: A recent study has unveiled that the activation of Gi/o protein-coupled receptors leads to the stimulation of Na+/K+ ATPase. This stimulation, in turn, hyperpolarizes the membrane potential of β-cells, consequently suppressing β-cell electrical excitability and insulin secretion (Dickerson et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dickerson et al., 2022
